pr_title: Fix doc building to use astropy source
pr_statement:
Fixing this was more subtle than I realized, but this PR now finally makes the sphinx build operate consistently.  Now, `python setup.py build_sphinx` always uses the version of astropy in the build directory, while `make html` in the `docs` directory will use the installed version.

As part of this, a critical bug is fixed that in the past meant you _had_ to have the C extensions installed via `python setup.py develop` or `python setup.py build_ext --inplace` to get the docs to build.  That is no longer the case.

This closes #134 .

change_discussion.discussion_summary: Reviewer `mdboom` reported that the documentation build output was placed in an incorrect nested directory (`docs/docs/_build/html`). Reviewer `embray` confirmed seeing the same behavior. The author (`eteq`) later acknowledged the issue, identified the cause as changing the directory within the subprocess (`os.chdir('docs')`) without properly handling relative paths, and provided a fix.
change_discussion.original_reviewer_comment: Very welcome change.  For me, `python setup.py build_sphinx` seems to dump the built docs into `docs/docs/_build/html` rather than `docs/_build/html`.  Any idea why?

-                subproccode[i] = repr(getattr(self, iden))
+                val = getattr(self, iden)
+                if iden.endswith('_dir'):
+                    #Directories should be absolute, because the `chdir` call
+                    #in the new process moves to a different directory
+                    subproccode[i] = repr(os.path.abspath(val))

change_resolve_info.resolution_explanation: The fix addresses the issue by ensuring that all directory paths (`iden` ending with `_dir`) passed into the subprocess code are converted to absolute paths using `os.path.abspath(val)`. This prevents the `os.chdir()` call within the subprocess from causing relative paths (like the build output directory) to be resolved incorrectly, thus ensuring the documentation is built in the intended `docs/_build/html` location instead of `docs/docs/_build/html`.

pr_timeline.body:
Fixing this was more subtle than I realized, but this PR now finally makes the sphinx build operate consistently.  Now, `python setup.py build_sphinx` always uses the version of astropy in the build directory, while `make html` in the `docs` directory will use the installed version.

As part of this, a critical bug is fixed that in the past meant you _had_ to have the C extensions installed via `python setup.py develop` or `python setup.py build_ext --inplace` to get the docs to build.  That is no longer the case.

This closes #134 .

pr_timeline.body: Well it's not `Header.fromtextfile` that's the problem.  So I don't know...

This behavior is inherited from wcslib.  See here:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/master/astropy/wcs/src/wcslib/C/wcshdr.h#L381

Admittedly, we should probably copy these notes to the Python documentation -- this issue has come up before for pywcs -- it's a little confusing but apparently how the WCS standard is supposed to work.

If I can paraphrase the reason I was told for this behavior:

It's possible that a WCS may want to specify extra dimensions while still having fewer dimensions in the actual data itself (which of course uses NAXIS).

Also, it is possible to limit the number of dimensions by passing naxis=2 to the constructor.

But for those kinds of datasets, why not have `NAXIS=4` and set `NAXIS3` and `NAXIS4` to 1?

I guess what confused me was that regardless of this behavior, I would have thought `wcs.naxis` should be equal to `NAXIS`, and I would also expect the _default_ behavior to be to accept `NAXIS` values for transformations. In the example where I ran into an issue, the 3rd and 4th dimensions were just residuals from a slicing algorithm which reduced `NAXIS` but forgot to remove the associated WCS keywords.

Wouldn't a more sensible behavior be to respect `NAXIS` by default, and allow the user to override it with `WCS(..., naxis=...)` which would cause the missing `NAXIS*` keywords to be set to 1 and the further WCS keywords to be read (with an exception being raised if they are missing). This would seem more natural to me. If further keywords are present compared to `NAXIS`, one could even raise an INFO message to let the user know they have the option to force naxis to a higher value.

There is justification for this behavior in Paper I, section 2.2.

http://www.atnf.csiro.au/people/mcalabre/WCS/wcs.pdf

(I suggest reading that section in its entirety, but it essentially amounts to "the addition of degenerate axes to otherwise n-dimensional data may mean some software will reject it unnecessarily").

None of this precludes what you're suggesting, but I'm wary to deviate from the behavior of wcslib unless there's something that can't be done any other way.  In this particular case, one can pass an explicit `naxis` kwarg to the constructor to force a requested number of axes.  However, there are some things we can do to make this easier on the user.  I propose:

1) Adding a warning when `NAXIS` < `naxis`

2) Changing `wcs.naxis` to be equal to the `NAXIS` FITS keyword is a bad idea.  It should match the number of axes in the transformation, not in the data.  And this is a class for WCS transformations, after all.  We have `io.fits`/`pyfits` to handle the dimensions of the data.

3) `naxis1` and `naxis2` should probably be made private (through some gradual deprecation perhaps, since that's backward-incompatible).  They are used pretty much exclusively by the footprint calculation which is 2D only.  Having them available here just causes confusion, and they really should be obtained directly from the dimensions of the data array in the pyfits HDU object.  I could also be persuaded here that we define `naxisX` for all `X` <= `wcs.naxis`, and the missing values are 1.  That would at least provide a consistent interface to get dimensions even when `naxis` > `NAXIS` and wouldn't force the use of degenerate axes in the FITS file itself.

EDIT: Changed != to < in proposal #1.

+def deprecated_attribute(name, since, message=None, alternative=None,

+    """
+    Used to mark a public attribute as deprecated.  This creates a
+    property that will warn when the given attribute name is accessed.

+            # Mark the old_name as deprecated
+            old_name = misc.deprecated_attribute('old_name', '0.1')
+
+            def method(self):
+                self._old_name = 42
+    """
+    private_name = '_' + name
+
+    @deprecated(since, name=name, obj_type='attribute')

+
+    return property(get, set, delete)

@iguananaut: I added a `deprecate_attribute` function that piggy backs on the `deprecate` decorator.  It's of course possible to do this by turning the attribute into a property and deprecating the property's methods, but this turns all of that into a one liner in the case where the property doesn't need to do anything special.  You might want to have a look as the original `@deprecate` author.

Yes.  This header was actually only working by "accident" -- the wcslib parser is fuzzy about FITS headers with carriage returns.  It doesn't complain -- it reads some cards that don't overlap an 80 character boundary and silently rejects others.  I didn't notice this problem with this header until, in this PR, the header needed to be re-parsed by `io.fits` in order to read the `NAXIS` card.

reply.body: Yes.  This header was actually only working by "accident" -- the wcslib parser is fuzzy about FITS headers with carriage returns.  It doesn't complain -- it reads some cards that don't overlap an 80 character boundary and silently rejects others.  I didn't notice this problem with this header until, in this PR, the header needed to be re-parsed by `io.fits` in order to read the `NAXIS` card.

pr_title: Add sections Getting help and Reporting issues to main doc index
pr_statement:
This adds information on getting help and reporting issues, expanding somewhat on the text from www.astropy.org. 

I think it's good to have this info on the landing page for astropy docs.  The Getting Started section is another candidate location that would make sense if people don't think this belongs on the main index.

Preview at http://hea-www.harvard.edu/~aldcroft/tmp/astropy/html/index.html

change_introducing.code_snippet:
docs/index.rst
@@ -65,6 +65,32 @@ testing guidelines.
     development/scripts
     development/sphinxext
 
+***********************
+Getting help
+***********************
+
+If you want to get help or discuss issues with other Astropy users, you can
+sign up for the `astropy <http://mail.scipy.org/mailman/listinfo/astropy>`_
+mailing list.  Alternatively, the `astropy-dev
+<http://groups.google.com/group/astropy-dev>`_ list is where you should go to
+discuss more technical aspects of Astropy with the developers.
+
+***********************
+Reporting issues
+***********************
+
+If you have come across something that you believe is a bug, please open a
+ticket in the Astropy `issue tracker
+<http://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues>`_, and we will look into it
+promptly.
+
+Please try to include an example that demonstrates the issue and will allow the
+developers to reproduce and fix the problem.  If you are seeing a crash
+then frequently it will help to include the full Python stack trace as well as
+information about your operating system (e.g. MacOSX version or Linux version).
+
+
+
 ******************
 Indices and Tables
 ******************

change_discussion.discussion_summary: Reviewer `astrofrog` suggested moving the newly added sections (introduced at the bottom of the page in commit 63b57a0) higher up, specifically suggesting placing them before the developer documentation or in the 'Getting started' section. Reviewer `embray` agreed. The author (`taldcroft`) discussed the options and acknowledged the suggestion by implementing the move in a subsequent commit.
change_discussion.original_reviewer_comment: This is a good idea! However, it should not be below the dev docs, as users will stop reading when they reach 'developer docs'. I agree it would make sense to put it in 'Getting started'.

results seem unlikely to change in refereeing given the maturity of their analysis.

from Hinshaw et al.  Because this paper hasn't yet been accepted, leave
WMAP7 as the default.  However, papers using WMAP9 are already starting
to appear, so it seems worth making it easy for users.  Plus, their cosmological
results seem unlikely to change in refereeing given the maturity of their analysis.

change_discussion.discussion_summary: Reviewer `eteq` pointed out that while `spectral_density` could handle energy units (`keV`) in its *argument*, it failed when trying to convert *to* a unit with an energy denominator (`erg/s/cm^2/keV`). This highlighted a missing piece of functionality required for X-ray astronomy units. Reviewer `pllim` later confirmed (2014-04-07T18:24:25) that this unit combination was indeed undefined within the existing `spectral_density` implementation and suggested expanding it.
change_discussion.original_reviewer_comment:
@astrofrog Aha, ok, yeah, that gets into some dangerous territory now that I see more closely and I'm okay with not doing that

re: the second one: (I tried to make a notebook about this and put it on http://nbviewer.ipython.org/9997406 , but at least as of this post it's not working, so I summarized below.  But by the time you read it, perhaps it will be up).  I see the following:

```
(1*u.Jy).to(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.AA,
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(4000 * u.AA))
(1*u.Jy).to(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.AA,
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(3.1e-3 * u.keV))
```

Both work as you'd expect, giving roughly the same answer: it treats 3.1e-3 keV (equivalent to 4000 angstroms) as the energy of the photon, and does the flux conversion to per-wavelength correctly.

But this does _not_ work:

```
(1*u.Jy).to(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.keV,
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(3.1e-3 * u.keV))
```

it gives me an error that the units aren't right... So is that supposed to be working now, then (and hence it's a bug)?

change_discussion.discussion_summary: Reviewer `eteq` questioned whether the `spectral_density` equivalency should work for units beyond the explicitly defined flux/luminosity densities (e.g., for integrated energy per spectral bin). This pointed out a limitation in the implementation's generality, suggesting it could be broadened to handle any compatible numerator unit while converting the spectral denominator (e.g., `/Hz` to `/AA`). The discussion confirmed this generalization was desirable but not implemented.
change_discussion.original_reviewer_comment:
Also, one other thing occurs to me about this,  @astrofrog.  Should this work:

```
(1*u.Jy * 600 * u.s * pi*10**2 * u.m**2).to(u.erg/u.AA,
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(4000 * u.AA))
```

That is, spectral density is useful for a variety of other numerator units.  Are we just going to say we only support flux numerators, or is there a way to generalize this to make it possible for things like energy?

pr_timeline.body: I've implemented as `ergs <-> photon` conversion. Before we implement any more, I'd like to understand why defining `ergs <-> photon` does not allow `ergs / s <-> photon / s` to work. Would it maybe make sense to make the equivalencies smarter? Then one would also not have to define power / area / spectral unit **and** power / spectral unit (the latter would be enough, because the area doesn't mattter). @mdboom - do you have any thoughts on this?

pr_timeline.body: @mdboom - thanks! I'm going to test this out now and will update this PR appropriately.

Hmm, I think this might be confusing:

```
In [12]: (1. * u.erg / u.cm**2 / u.s / u.Hz).to(u.erg / u.cm**2 / u.s / u.micron,
                equivalencies=u.spectral())
Out[12]: <Quantity 299792458.0 erg / (cm2 micron s)>

In [14]: (1. * u.erg / u.cm**2 / u.s / u.Hz).to(u.erg / u.cm**2 / u.s / u.micron,
                equivalencies=u.spectral_density(u.micron, 1.))
Out[14]: <Quantity 299792457999999.94 erg / (cm2 micron s)>
```

In other words, the result is different in both cases, because in the first case, the conversion is assumed to be straight from the wavelength to frequency, while in the second case the /Hz and /micron refer to an interval, which depends on the frequency/wavelength assumed. I'm not sure if there's a way around that unfortunately. Of course, the user is getting what they are asking for because they should choose the equivalencies wisely, but I'm not sure if they will... Any ideas? Or maybe we just have to hard-code the conversions, but make use of loops to make it easier to cycle through the combinations (there's a finite number of sensible ones).

Whether we merge this or not, I'd like to merge 6d496f5 which allows for the application of equivalencies to just part of a decomposed unit.  Any objections, or do you think this PR will be revived soon enough...?
@mdboom - I think we still need to think a lot more about this PR, so feel free to merge that specific commit separately.
@mdboom - please go ahead and merge https://github.com/astropy/astropy/commit/6d496f5 manually, and I'm going to reassign this issue to 0.4.0

I think this should just be closed. For instance, I don't think we should have an equivalency for ergs/cm^2/s -> ergs/cm^2/s/Hz since that is just a different unit and one can get to it by doing `F / nu`. If no-one has objections to closing, I will do so in the next few days.

cc @pllim @perrygreenfield - since this may related to pysynphot - and @eteq

@astrofrog - I'm a bit confused which equivalencies are in discussion here, actually.  The following I think are important:
- erg <-> photons (this could be a separate, independent equivalency, though? `u.photon_energy`, perhaps?)
- have the existing spectral_density support _energy_, both as the argument, and as the denominator of the unit.  E.g.:`(1*u.Jy).to(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.keV, equivalencies=u.spectral_density(10*u.keV))` because of course this is very common in x-ray work.  In principal it's _easier_. because it's just an scaling of `Hz` by `h`, right?

Or is there something you're saying that prevents one or both of these?

@eteq - the original one here was also addressing things like ergs/cm^2/s -> ergs/cm^2/Hz which I think is more dangerous. But I agree that the ones you are mentioning should be done (and I thought the second should already work with the spectral equivalency?)

@astrofrog Aha, ok, yeah, that gets into some dangerous territory now that I see more closely and I'm okay with not doing that

re: the second one: (I tried to make a notebook about this and put it on http://nbviewer.ipython.org/9997406 , but at least as of this post it's not working, so I summarized below.  But by the time you read it, perhaps it will be up).  I see the following:

```
(1*u.Jy).to(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.AA, 
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(4000 * u.AA))
(1*u.Jy).to(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.AA, 
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(3.1e-3 * u.keV))
```

Both work as you'd expect, giving roughly the same answer: it treats 3.1e-3 keV (equivalent to 4000 angstroms) as the energy of the photon, and does the flux conversion to per-wavelength correctly.

But this does _not_ work:

```
(1*u.Jy).to(u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.keV, 
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(3.1e-3 * u.keV))
```

it gives me an error that the units aren't right... So is that supposed to be working now, then (and hence it's a bug)?
Well, my personal guess is that it should work because it's just a combination of spectral_density and spectral, although maybe @mdboom could clarify whether the last example you showed should work?

The problem that @eteq illustrated is because `u.erg/u.s/u.cm**2/u.keV` is undefined as a flux unit in `spectral_density()` equivalencies. IMHO, the solution is to expand `spectral_density()` to include that with relevant converters.
Ah, so just adding an equivalency to map energy / time / area / energy (= 1/time/area) to energy / time / area / freq should make it work, is that right, @pllim ?

Also, one other thing occurs to me about this,  @astrofrog.  Should this work:

```
(1*u.Jy * 600 * u.s * pi*10**2 * u.m**2).to(u.erg/u.AA, 
            equivalencies=u.spectral_density(4000 * u.AA))
```

That is, spectral density is useful for a variety of other numerator units.  Are we just going to say we only support flux numerators, or is there a way to generalize this to make it possible for things like energy?
@eteq , theoretically, yes. That's how I got PHOTLAM and PHOTNU conversions to work in `spectral_density()`.

So can that be done more generally?  E.g., make it such that this works for _any_ `numer_unit`?:

```
(1 * numer_unit / u.Hz).to(numer_unit/u.AA, equivalencies=u.spectral_density(4000 * u.AA))
```

Or is this what you were objecting to, @astrofrog? (I don't think it is, because this still enforces that the _numerator_ stays the same)
Going through some old pull requests.  As master now has a `spectral_denstity` equivalency, isn't this obsolete?  Closing -- but feel free to reopen if I'm wrong.
Nevermind -- I'm wrong!  Sorry for the noise.

@mdboom @pllim - I'm going through old issues and I want to wrap this one up. But first I want to understand why the spectral density equivalency includes certain lines in master. These make sense:

```
        (fla, fnu, converter, iconverter),
        (fnu, nufnu, converter_fnu_nufnu, iconverter_fnu_nufnu),
        (fla, lafla, converter_fla_lafla, iconverter_fla_lafla),
        (photlam, fla, converter_photlam_fla, iconverter_photlam_fla),
        (photlam, fnu, converter_photlam_fnu, iconverter_photlam_fnu),
        (photlam, photnu, converter_photlam_photnu, iconverter_photlam_photnu),
        (photnu, fnu, converter_photnu_fnu, iconverter_photnu_fnu),
        (photnu, fla, converter_photnu_fla, iconverter_photnu_fla)
```

But these don't:

```
        (si.AA, fnu, converter, iconverter),
        (si.AA, si.Hz, converter, iconverter),
        (fla, si.Hz, converter, iconverter),
```

Specifically, wavelengths and frequencies are not units of spectral density, so why do we include those?

I am not very sure. By the time I added stuff to this equivalency, the 3 lines in question were already there:

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/commit/2305a7482032fd811e942bdf6aea963f6588a7cb#diff-4

https://github.com/astropy/astropy/commit/7d1f0e4a568787132d8d3d67f9e889f3e9eada29
@pllim - indeed, and you had commented on it at the time! I think those lines should be removed. @mdboom, can you confirm?

@astrofrog - in the spirit of the mailing list discussion, I assigned this to myself. Looking at the PR, there really seem to be two parts, one somewhat reworking the units core, the other rewriting the equivalencies. It is probably the former that prevents merging, since the equivalency part of `core.py` has been changed.  Would it be an idea to split this PR in two pieces?

@mhvk - looking back on this, I think that we should _not_ add equivalencies for fnu -> nu*fnu (see https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/692#issuecomment-12802323). The user can do that themselves. However, I think what might still be useful is the conversion including photons. I'll look into that.

Also, I'm not sure if @mdboom went ahead and merged 6d496f5  manually (can try and check later)
The photon equivalencies were added by @pllim in https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/1560 - so this issue is now moot :)
I like it when I read things like this on a Monday! :)
